title: Finding a Gene’s Message in Tissue
endLine: A matching probe marks where a gene’s RNA is present.

scenes.tts: Which cells in the retina carry a gene's message? The retina is the layered tissue lining the back of the eye. The cells are still in their places, but their messages are too small to see. We need a way to mark where a particular message is.
scenes.caption: Which cells in the retina carry a gene's message? The retina is the layered tissue lining the back of the eye. The cells are still in their places, but their messages are too small to see. We need a way to mark where a particular message is.
scenes.visual: Open on a schematic full-height stack of retina layers with cell silhouettes and a question mark travelling across the layers under the opening question. On 'inside the eye', briefly pull back to the schematic eye and trace the section along the back inside edge of the eye. Zoom back into the same section and carry it through the film. Throughout, show a visible 'schematic' label, use gray for tissue, blue for RNA and yellow for the probe and its signal. Keep labels large and high contrast. Let the section fill most of the frame height. After the hook, allow the motion to lead the narration and continue through each transition. Pace these transitions for the web runtime.
scenes.narration: Which cells in the retina carry a gene's message? The retina is the layered tissue lining the back of the eye. The cells are still in their places, but their messages are too small to see. We need a way to mark where a particular message is.

scenes.tts: Zoom into a cell to follow the message. A cell can make a message from a gene. Making that message is part of gene expression. The message is called messenger R N A. Here, we want to find the cells where that message is present.
scenes.caption: Zoom into a cell to follow the message. A cell can make a message from a gene. Making that message is part of gene expression. The message is called messenger RNA. Here, we want to find the cells where that message is present.
scenes.visual: Keep the schematic retina at the edge of the zoom so the cell stays anchored to its layer. Enlarge a cell silhouette. Slide a blue tile into view beside a neutral tile labelled 'Gene', then label the blue tile 'Messenger RNA' as it moves within the cell. Use flat tiles, with no molecular detail.
scenes.narration: Zoom into a cell to follow the message. A cell can make a message from a gene. Making that message is part of gene expression. The message is called messenger RNA. Here, we want to find the cells where that message is present.

scenes.tts: To find the message, experimenters add a matching piece called a probe. The probe carries a label so we can see where it stays. When it meets the matching R N A, the two bind, and unbound probes are washed away.
scenes.caption: To find the message, experimenters add a matching piece called a probe. The probe carries a label so we can see where it stays. When it meets the matching RNA, the two bind, and unbound probes are washed away.
scenes.visual: Into the same schematic cell close-up, slide a flat tile labelled 'Probe' with a yellow spot attached. Let the spot pulse once as the label is explained. Bring the blue RNA tile and probe tile together so their simple edges meet. Use abstract tiles throughout. Wash any unbound probe tiles out of the cell after pairing.
scenes.narration: To find the message, experimenters add a matching piece called a probe. The probe carries a label so we can see where it stays. When it meets the matching RNA, the two bind, and unbound probes are washed away.

scenes.tts: That pairing is called hybridization, and in situ means in place. Together, in situ hybridization marks R N A while cells stay in place in the tissue. As we zoom back out, the marks give us a map of where the message is present.
scenes.caption: That pairing is called hybridization, and in situ means in place. Together, in situ hybridization marks RNA while cells stay in place in the tissue. As we zoom back out, the marks give us a map of where the message is present.
scenes.visual: Start with the bound tiles in the same schematic cell. Pull back smoothly, letting the pair shrink to a yellow mark anchored inside that cell. Several similarly marked cells come into view as the section fills the frame again. Keep the marks attached to cell locations through the zoom.
scenes.narration: That pairing is called hybridization, and in situ means in place. Together, in situ hybridization marks RNA while cells stay in place in the tissue. As we zoom back out, the marks give us a map of where the message is present.

scenes.tts: Let's use that rule to read the retina. Imagine the message is present only in cells in the inner layers. Picture the probe meeting its match there. When you zoom out and look at the whole section, where would you expect the marks to appear?
scenes.caption: Let's use that rule to read the retina. Imagine the message is present only in cells in the inner layers. Picture the probe meeting its match there. When you zoom out and look at the whole section, where would you expect the marks to appear?
scenes.visual: Clear the schematic marks and briefly bring blue RNA tiles into view in inner-layer cells. Let the tiles shrink out of view as the drawing pulls back to the whole section. Place an open question mark beside the section and show 'Where will marks appear?' Keep all probe signal hidden. Label that side of the stack 'Inner layers'.
scenes.narration: Let's use that rule to read the retina. Imagine the message is present only in cells in the inner layers. Picture the probe meeting its match there. When you zoom out and look at the whole section, where would you expect the marks to appear?

scenes.visual: Hold the schematic retina and 'Where will marks appear?' in place for the thinking pause. Keep the answer hidden.

scenes.tts: The marks would appear in the inner layers, because that is where the probe has a match. Now imagine looking for the same message with the wrong probe. You could miss the message even in cells where it really is present.
scenes.caption: The marks would appear in the inner layers, because that is where the probe has a match. Now imagine looking for the same message with the wrong probe. You could miss the message even in cells where it really is present.
scenes.visual: Reveal schematic yellow marks inside the inner layers. Zoom into a marked cell, separate the tiles and move the original probe away. Slide in a tile labelled 'Wrong probe' and bring it past the blue RNA tile without pairing. Keep the blue tile visible as the probe leaves.
scenes.narration: The marks would appear in the inner layers, because that is where the probe has a match. Now imagine looking for the same message with the wrong probe. You could miss the message even in cells where it really is present.

scenes.tts: So check that the probe matches the message you mean to find. Even with the right probe, the map shows only location. Having an R N A message alone does not make a cell light-sensitive. Testing light responses takes a separate recording in living cells.
scenes.caption: So check that the probe matches the message you mean to find. Even with the right probe, the map shows only location. Having an RNA message alone does not make a cell light-sensitive. Testing light responses takes a separate recording in living cells.
scenes.visual: In the same schematic cell, bring back the matching probe and pair the tiles. Pull out to the marked section and add the label 'Location only'. Then shift to a separate unstained schematic retina labelled 'Separate living test', sweep a pale band labelled 'Light' across it, and bring in an empty frame labelled 'Record a response', leaving the response unknown.
scenes.narration: So check that the probe matches the message you mean to find. Even with the right probe, the map shows only location. Having an RNA message alone does not make a cell light-sensitive. Testing light responses takes a separate recording in living cells.

scenes.tts: In two thousand, Provencio and colleagues used this method to map a gene called melanopsin. They tested retinal tissue from adult macaque and from adult and ten day old mice. Marks appeared in the inner retina, in the ganglion and amacrine cell layers, with no light response recorded.
scenes.caption: In 2000, Provencio and colleagues used this method to map a gene called melanopsin. They tested retinal tissue from adult macaque and from adult and 10-day-old mice. Marks appeared in the inner retina, in the ganglion and amacrine cell layers, with no light response recorded.
scenes.visual: Clear the practice signal and use the same schematic section to show sequential sample labels 'Adult macaque', 'Adult mice' and '10-day-old mice'. Replace the sample labels with 'Melanopsin RNA', then bring up yellow marks within the two inner-retina bands, with 'Ganglion cell layer' innermost and 'Amacrine cell layer' beside it. Convey locations without precise cell counts or densities.
scenes.narration: In 2000, Provencio and colleagues used this method to map a gene called melanopsin. They tested retinal tissue from adult macaque and from adult and 10-day-old mice. Marks appeared in the inner retina, in the ganglion and amacrine cell layers, with no light response recorded.

scenes.tts: In twenty nineteen, Peng and colleagues profiled cells from adult macaque retinas. To check which cells each group matched, they used fluorescent in situ hybridization. Fluorescent means the probe's label gives off light, making marks visible.
scenes.caption: In 2019, Peng and colleagues profiled cells from adult macaque retinas. To check which cells each group matched, they used fluorescent in situ hybridization. Fluorescent means the probe's label gives off light, making marks visible.
scenes.visual: Clear the melanopsin marks and return to the adult macaque schematic. Bring the retina label 'Adult macaque' into view before zooming into cells, then let yellow probe marks brighten inside the silhouettes as the label gives off light. Use representative cells without assigning an invented marker pattern to a named cell type.
scenes.narration: In 2019, Peng and colleagues profiled cells from adult macaque retinas. To check which cells each group matched, they used fluorescent in situ hybridization. Fluorescent means the probe's label gives off light, making marks visible.

scenes.tts: Peng and colleagues also used a virus to label cell shapes. Together, the fluorescent marks and shapes checked the identities of two ganglion cell groups, called midget and parasol.
scenes.caption: Peng and colleagues also used a virus to label cell shapes. Together, the fluorescent marks and shapes checked the identities of two ganglion cell groups, called midget and parasol.
scenes.visual: Carry the same schematic cell silhouettes and yellow marks. As the shapes are labelled, trace their outlines with a green overlay reserved for cell shape. Pull back into the full retina section as both layers of evidence stay visible. Bring up the paired labels 'Midget' and 'Parasol' beside the schematic without assigning either type an invented shape or marker pattern.
scenes.narration: Peng and colleagues also used a virus to label cell shapes. Together, the fluorescent marks and shapes checked the identities of two ganglion cell groups, called midget and parasol.

scenes.visual: The schematic retina recedes into the background while the yellow marks remain visible. Set the end line in high-contrast type: A matching probe marks where a gene’s RNA is present.
